course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

writingQuizzes.title: LEQ: Did economic change create a national identity?

topic.title: Expanding Democracy
topic.summary: How voting expanded from property owners to nearly all adult white men between 1800 and 1848, how party politics changed as a result, and who was left out.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: By the 1840s, which of the following was true of voting qualifications in most states?
choices: Property requirements had been replaced by literacy tests for all white men
Free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men in most states
Property requirements for white men had been dropped
Women who owned property could vote in local elections in most states
questions.explanation: New states entered with few restrictions and older states revised their constitutions, so most white men could vote without owning property.
choiceExplanations: Literacy tests became common much later.
Many states restricted or denied the vote to free Black men.
New states entered with few restrictions and older states revised their constitutions, so most white men could vote without owning property.
Women could not vote in most states.
questions.distinguisher: The literacy test choice is close because it also replaced property tests in some states later, but not in the 1840s.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The Anti-Masonic Party's national convention in 1831 was significant because it
choices: established the first national political party in the history of the United States
introduced the nominating convention that other parties then adopted
ended the use of the Electoral College as a method of choosing presidents
marked the first time that the House of Representatives chose a president
questions.explanation: Conventions replaced congressional caucuses and gave parties a more open way to name candidates.
choiceExplanations: National parties had existed since the 1790s.
Conventions replaced congressional caucuses and gave parties a more open way to name candidates.
The Electoral College remained.
The House first chose a president in 1801.
questions.distinguisher: The first party choice is close because the Anti-Masonic Party was a new party, but the Federalists and Democratic-Republicans came earlier.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains the movement to end property requirements for voting?
choices: Wage earners without land and new western states pressed for an equal political voice
Wealthy landowners demanded a larger electorate to protect their estates from taxes
Congress ordered every state to change its constitution by passing a federal law
The Supreme Court ruled that property requirements violated the First Amendment
questions.explanation: Men who paid taxes and served in the militia argued that they deserved a vote, and competing parties sought their support.
choiceExplanations: Men who paid taxes and served in the militia argued that they deserved a vote, and competing parties sought their support.
Landowners generally defended the older requirements.
States decided their own voting rules.
The Court did not make such a ruling.
questions.distinguisher: The landowners choice is close because some wealthy leaders supported change, but the pressure came from workers and the West.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Jackson's supporters charged a “corrupt bargain” after the election of 1824 because
choices: the Senate refused to count the electoral votes that had given Jackson a majority
Clay had withdrawn from the race and then received a cabinet post from Jackson
Adams had won the most popular votes, but the Supreme Court awarded the office to Jackson
Adams, chosen by the House, named Clay secretary of state although Jackson led in votes
questions.explanation: Since no candidate won a majority, the House decided the election, and the appointment of Clay looked like a deal to Jackson's supporters.
choiceExplanations: No candidate had a majority of the electoral votes.
Clay received the cabinet post from Adams.
The House, and not the Court, chose the president.
Since no candidate won a majority, the House decided the election, and the appointment of Clay looked like a deal to Jackson's supporters.
questions.distinguisher: The Senate choice is close because the Senate counts electoral votes, but no one had a majority in 1824.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes voter turnout in presidential elections between 1824 and 1840?
choices: It fell as property requirements ended and fewer men saw a reason to vote
It rose sharply, from about a quarter of eligible voters to about eighty percent
It stayed near one-half of the electorate in each election during these years
It rose among women, who voted in large numbers in the election of 1840
questions.explanation: Mass campaigns and a larger electorate raised participation to a very high level by 1840.
choiceExplanations: Turnout increased.
Mass campaigns and a larger electorate raised participation to a very high level by 1840.
Turnout changed dramatically.
Women could not vote.
questions.distinguisher: The steady-turnout choice is close because turnout was about half in 1828, but it was lower in 1824 and higher in 1840.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following limited the expansion of democracy in the early 1800s?
choices: Congress banned white men without property from voting in federal elections
State constitutions required every voter to join a political party and to pay dues
Many states took the vote away from free Black men while giving it to all white men
Federal courts ended elections in the Western territories until they became states
questions.explanation: As white men gained the vote, states such as Pennsylvania took it from free Black men, and women and American Indians stayed outside.
choiceExplanations: The states controlled voting qualifications.
No state required party membership.
As white men gained the vote, states such as Pennsylvania took it from free Black men, and women and American Indians stayed outside.
Territorial elections continued.
questions.distinguisher: The federal ban choice is close because Congress did set some rules for territories, but voting rights were set by the states.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference in voting rights in the 1830s?
choices: Free Black men could vote in every state, while white men needed property to vote
White women could vote in most states, while free Black women could not
American Indians voted in all states, while white men needed to own property
Most states ended property tests for white men but many limited free Black men
questions.explanation: Democracy grew for white men, but free Black men lost or never gained equal voting rights in many states.
choiceExplanations: The rights were reversed.
White women could not vote in most states.
American Indians were not citizens and could not vote.
Democracy grew for white men, but free Black men lost or never gained equal voting rights in many states.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed-rights choice is close because it uses the same two groups, but white men had broader rights.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The growth of party rallies, parades, and campaign newspapers is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A larger electorate that parties had to reach and persuade across many states
A federal ban on private political organizations that forced parties to work in secret
A decline in voter interest that led parties to hold events to keep their members
The end of the Electoral College and the direct election of the president by Congress
questions.explanation: As more men could vote, parties turned to mass campaigns to win them.
choiceExplanations: As more men could vote, parties turned to mass campaigns to win them.
No such ban existed.
Voter interest grew.
The Electoral College remained.
questions.distinguisher: The declining interest choice is close because campaigns were designed to raise interest, but participation was growing.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the main argument that Tocqueville makes in the excerpt?
choices: Nations that widen the right to vote usually return to property requirements after a short time
Once a nation begins to widen the right to vote, it will not stop short of giving it to all
Wealthy voters will always protect their power by preventing any extension of the vote
A nation can safely extend the vote to some groups and then stop the process
questions.explanation: Tocqueville says that after each concession the democracy gains strength and its demands increase, until universal suffrage is reached.
choiceExplanations: He says the process rarely reverses.
Tocqueville says that after each concession the democracy gains strength and its demands increase, until universal suffrage is reached.
He says the push for wider voting grows stronger.
He argues that no stop can be made.
questions.distinguisher: The safe-stopping choice is close because it addresses the same process, but Tocqueville says that stopping is not possible.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.7, KC-4.1.I: the nation moved to a more participatory democracy by expanding suffrage from a system based on property ownership to one based on voting by all adult white men
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Alexis de Tocqueville, a French writer who traveled in the United States in 1831–1832, in Democracy in America, published in 1835
stimulusBlocks.citation: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835), chap. 4, translated by Henry Reeve. Project Gutenberg eBook #815.
stimulusBlocks.note: The “elective qualification” is the requirement that voters own property or pay taxes. By “universal suffrage” Tocqueville means voting by all adult white men, because women, most African Americans, and American Indians could not vote in most states.
stimulusBlocks.text: When a nation modifies the elective qualification, it may easily be foreseen that sooner or later that qualification will be entirely abolished. There is no more invariable rule in the history of society: the further electoral rights are extended, the greater is the need of extending them; for after each concession the strength of the democracy increases, and its demands increase with its strength. The ambition of those who are below the appointed rate is irritated in exact proportion to the great number of those who are above it. The exception at last becomes the rule, concession follows concession, and no stop can be made short of universal suffrage.

questions.subskillText: Identify the evidence used in a source to support an argument.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Tocqueville's observations are useful to historians of American democracy?
choices: He was an elected official who helped to write the state constitutions of the 1820s
He was a former president who had directed the changes in suffrage after 1800
He was a foreign traveler who compared the United States with Europe
He was a Southern planter whose experience shows the views of the enslaved
questions.explanation: An observer from another society could notice patterns that Americans took for granted, though his account reflects his own point of view.
choiceExplanations: He was a visitor from France and not an American official.
He was never president of the United States.
An observer from another society could notice patterns that Americans took for granted, though his account reflects his own point of view.
He was not a planter, and he wrote as a French traveler.
questions.distinguisher: The official choice is close because he wrote about politics, but he was a French visitor and not a participant in American government.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments before 1835 best illustrates the trend Tocqueville describes?
choices: Congress passed a law that gave the vote to women who owned property in every state
Southern states ended slavery in order to give the right to vote to more people
The Supreme Court ruled that all citizens had an equal right to vote in federal elections
New western states and older states dropped property requirements for white men
questions.explanation: The extension of the vote to white men without property is the trend that Tocqueville describes.
choiceExplanations: Congress did not give women the vote.
Southern states did not end slavery in these years.
No such ruling was made.
The extension of the vote to white men without property is the trend that Tocqueville describes.
questions.distinguisher: The women's vote choice is close because it also describes an extension of voting, but it did not occur in this period.
